# Recover a desktop start

This guide is for a packaged Station desktop app that stays hidden while it
starts, says **Station is taking longer than usual to start**, or opens but
then cannot reach its local service. It describes the recovery behavior implemented in the desktop
host; it is not evidence that every platform's packaged app has been exercised.
Contributor and operator procedures are in the repository's
[native shell verification guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/guides/native-shell-verification.md).

## What a normal packaged start does

Stable, Beta, and Nightly configure their main desktop window to start hidden.
For a Desktop-owned sidecar, the native host proves its exact generation,
instance ID, boot ID, and local API base. Revealing application content also
requires the main renderer to have mounted. The native shell starts the
identity proof; the renderer separately reports that it mounted. An old ticket
cannot reveal a newer sidecar.

If an installed service owns the home, or Desktop owns no sidecar, the host can
instead reveal the mounted connection/recovery surface. That does not establish
that a backend is reachable or ready. On macOS, an activation request can make
a native startup cover visible while readiness is pending. It shows the app
icon and **Starting Station**, and it does not expose application content.

This avoids showing a usable-looking window before its protected local surface
is ready. The original native-startup work is recorded in
[archive#3808](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/3808).

The short Station intro is separate from native readiness. If it has already
started visibly, a ready app finishes the name reveal and fades into the
workspace. It does not wait for a loading-animation cycle. Fast starts can skip
an unseen intro; reduced motion and recovery screens do not wait for it. Bringing
an existing window back or changing Stations does not replay the intro.

## When the window does not appear

A cold start can take longer than 30 seconds on a slow or busy computer. If
readiness has not completed after a 30-second startup epoch, Station keeps
starting and offers a choice once for that epoch:

- On macOS, the startup cover changes to **Station is taking longer than usual
  to start.** with **Restart** and **Quit** buttons. Return selects
  **Restart**; with keyboard navigation turned on, Tab moves between the two
  buttons and Space presses the focused one. Escape does nothing. While the
  cover is shown, typing and editing shortcuts are ignored; the Quit, Close,
  Hide and Minimize shortcuts still work, including on non-Latin keyboard
  layouts (where they use the key positions of a US keyboard). Closing the window only hides it: Station keeps starting, and the
  window comes back when you open Station again (Dock, launching it, or the
  tray). If Station was launched in the background (tray-only), this message
  appears when you open the window. If the cover cannot be shown, the dialog
  described next appears instead; it can stay open after the window appears,
  and its buttons are then ignored.
- On Windows and Linux, a **Station is taking longer than usual to start**
  dialog offers **Restart**, **Quit** and **Keep Waiting**. Closing it or
  pressing Escape is the same as **Keep Waiting**; only **Quit** closes the app.
  After **Keep Waiting**, the message comes back after 30 seconds, then 60,
  then every 2 minutes while Station still has not finished starting.

You do not have to choose. Desktop does not stop its local service when the
30 seconds pass. When the service finishes starting, the window opens without
any action from you (unless Station was launched in the background, or you
closed the window while waiting), and the macOS cover and its buttons
disappear. While that window is still waiting to open there is no time limit
on the service starting, including on a first launch, when Station creates
this computer's local connection only after the service is running. If the service fails instead,
waiting does not help: the **Restart** and **Quit** choices above still appear
when the 30 seconds pass, and Restart starts it again and lets Station finish
opening. If Station's window is already open (for example after you reload it,
or in a separate workspace window), it shows Station's recovery screen right
away if the service has stopped or failed, and after about a minute if the
service is still starting or restarting. On
Windows and Linux, the dialog
can stay open after the window appears; its buttons are then ignored. On
macOS, activating the app (Dock, second launch, deep link) shows the cover
again but does not restart anything.

- **Restart** starts a new epoch. With a current owned-sidecar ticket, the
  first restart rechecks that ticket without restarting a potentially healthy
  backend. If that recheck does not complete and you choose Restart again, or
  no current ticket exists, Desktop asks its bounded supervisor to restart the
  sidecar. If a durable service owns the home, or no sidecar is owned, it
  re-establishes the local recovery screen, which opens once the app has
  loaded; it does not start or restart the durable service.
- **Quit** closes the desktop app if that startup is still waiting. It does
  not reset data or remove a service.
- **Keep Waiting** closes the message and lets startup continue; the message
  returns later (30 seconds, then 60, then every 2 minutes) while startup is
  still waiting.
- After an unexpected exit, the supervisor can respawn the sidecar four times,
  after 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds. The fifth counted exit is terminal and reports
  failure. An owned-sidecar restart resets that attempt count; a ticket-only
  recheck does not. Neither proves that the underlying cause is fixed. The cap
  and fail-closed classification are covered by the linked native-startup work.

If the message reappears after a restart, stop restarting blindly and
collect the bounded diagnostics below. A data-home schema error containing
`STATION_HOME_RESET_REQUIRED` is deliberately fail-closed: restart attempts do
not repair it. Follow the exact `station home reset` conditions only after you
have a backup and have selected the intended home.

Some home or schema refusals occur before the supervisor starts. They show a
separate **Exit**-only dialog and start no backend. Repeatedly launching the app
does not repair the refused home.

If Station's built-in Node component cannot start, its dialog asks you to
reinstall the app. A helper timeout has a separate message: exit and try again,
then collect desktop logs if it continues. A timeout alone does not establish
that the installed component is damaged.

## Missing saved connections

If Station finds an existing shared folder without its saved `profiles.json` connection list, it
shows the folder and a bounded list of existing entry names. Restore the file
from backup if you previously saved connections. Station does not infer that
connections were never saved merely because the file is absent.

For a folder containing only inspected runtime bookkeeping, with no profile,
backup, cutover, or credential history, Desktop can offer **Create connection
list and restart**. This creates an empty list and preserves runtime data. The
checks run again after confirmation and under the shared locks. A marker from
an earlier initialization, an unknown lock, unreadable evidence, or saved
credentials keeps recovery at **Exit** only. This includes Station credentials
elsewhere in the current OS account's credential store, even if they belong to
another Station folder. Restore a known backup of the connection list before
relaunching; if no backup is available, keep the folder intact and collect the
diagnostics below for operator recovery. A separate
[recovery flow for users without a backup](https://github.com/kontourai/station/issues/4023)
is being designed; it is not available in the current app. An existing list is
never replaced.
Windows checks the raw Credential Manager target names, macOS checks service
metadata, and Linux requests only Station's items by service attribute. Unlocking
a requested item may unlock its whole collection in the desktop keyring. An inspection error never counts as an empty store.
Regular OS metadata files such as `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, and `desktop.ini` do
not prevent first initialization; symlinks and directories with those names do.

Installed desktop releases include Node. A message that this built-in
component could not start calls for reinstalling the desktop app, rather than
resetting its data folder or installing a different system Node.

## Check the local diagnosis

From the Station checkout or installed command, run:

```sh
station doctor
station service status --json
```

From a checkout, `station doctor` checks local prerequisites and readiness.
The packaged CLI reports the selected endpoint, its reachability, saved
credential state and configured local service. Neither form inspects a Tauri
renderer or proves that a packaged window was shown. `station service
status --json` checks an installed user service and its identity endpoints. It
does not diagnose a Desktop-owned sidecar, and its failure does not by itself
explain a hidden window.

Keep shell and service logs separate:

| What you need | macOS | Linux | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Desktop shell log | `~/Library/Logs/<app-identifier>/station.log` | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/<app-identifier>/logs/station.log`, or `~/.local/share/<app-identifier>/logs/station.log` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<app-identifier>\logs\station.log` |
| Desktop shell panic record | `crash.log` beside `station.log` | `crash.log` beside `station.log` | `crash.log` beside `station.log` |
| Installed service log | `<STATION_HOME>/logs/<instance>-service.out.log` and `<STATION_HOME>/logs/<instance>-service.err.log` | `journalctl --user -u station-<instance>.service` (no service log file) | `<STATION_HOME>/logs/<instance>-service.log` |

Choose the app identifier for your installed channel (Stable, Beta, or Nightly)
from the [channel log path table in the repository guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/guides/native-shell-verification.md).

The desktop shell honors `STATION_DESKTOP_LOG_LEVEL` set before launch:
`trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, or `off`. Its file rotation is
configured for up to five archived files plus the active log, with a 5 MiB
rotation threshold. This is not a hard file-size or total-size cap: an oversized
log entry can exceed the threshold. If the shell log directory is unwritable,
the host falls back to stdout. The server logging configuration is maintained
with the installed app. Logs can contain local data or secrets; redact them
before sharing.

## Second launches and the tray

An interactive second desktop launch, a reviewed deep link, and the macOS
reopen event ask the existing app to activate its main window. A background or
tray-only launch can suppress activation. While readiness is pending, content
reveal is deferred; macOS may show the native startup cover described above.
Once ready, the same reveal authority focuses the window.

The tray is a different surface: it reports the currently selected local
backend. For an installed service it can offer service actions; for a
Desktop-owned sidecar it labels the built-in service and does not use service
controls. Neither a tray click nor a second launch proves that startup readiness
completed.

## Evidence limits and open platform work

The source and focused tests cover state transitions and browser-renderer
logic. There is also a separate Tauri-WebView hostile-plugin harness. Its
existence is not a successful run: browser tests, source checks and an available
native harness must not be presented as packaged or physical-device evidence.

| Behavior | Current evidence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hidden release window, exact ticket, slow-start recovery, late reveal, restart, and activation deferral | Source configuration and pure Rust/UI test coverage associated with archive#3808 | **NOT_VERIFIED** on packaged macOS, Windows, and Linux shells |
| Hostile plugin IPC denial in a real Tauri WebView | Separate browser and real-WebView harnesses exist; the native lane was not run for this documentation review | **NOT_VERIFIED** here; historical gap recorded in [archive#2495](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/2495) |
| Renderer/WebView death detection and bounded reload | Window recreation exists; no automatic renderer-death recovery or kill-the-WebView proof is established here | **NOT_VERIFIED**; [archive#2006](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/2006) |
| EPIPE/closed-stdio handling | Server stdout guard and focused tests exist; no packaged closed-parent recovery journey was run here | **NOT_VERIFIED** on packaged shells; [archive#2006](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/2006) |
| macOS Finder/Dock Apple Event launch panic diagnosis | The historical abort report does not establish a recoverable panic payload or current trigger. The shell now appends Rust panics to `crash.log`, and that recording is unit-tested, but no packaged abort has been observed producing an entry | **NOT_VERIFIED**; [archive#3496](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/3496) |
| Tray rendering, tray activation, and second-launch behavior on release builds | Pure-state/static routing associated with [archive#3808](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/3808) | **NOT_VERIFIED** on packaged macOS, Windows, and Linux |
| Mobile startup and recovery | Desktop readiness code is desktop-only; no equivalent mobile recovery evidence is supplied here | **NOT_VERIFIED** on Android and iOS; historical documentation scope in [archive#3817](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/3817) |

The related implementation history is
[archive#3808](https://github.com/kontourai/station-archive/issues/3808). An
archived issue's status does not establish current implementation or release
qualification; use the owning source, tests and exact platform receipts.

documents.title: Pull request guides
documents.markdown:
# Pull request guides

A guide is an AI-written reading tour of a pull request, shared by everyone
using the same Station server. It explains the change in stops, with code
excerpts, files, questions, and occasional **Look closely** decisions.

In **Settings → Agent runs**, enable **Review guides** and choose a **Review
guide model**. An empty model uses the server's structure model. The configured
model must be available through Station's managed model connections. Generating
a guide sends the pull request's title, diff, and bounded changed-file context
to that model. **Review guide instructions** change emphasis and reading order;
they cannot remove file coverage or change excerpt validation.

Open a pull request in the Pull Requests pane, choose **Guide**, then **Write
guide**. Generation continues while you visit another tab. Return to inspect
progress or a failure, and move through the stops with **Previous** and **Next**.
Use **Rewrite guide** to try again or incorporate a new revision or preference.
Ordinary requests reuse a guide for the current head; Rewrite explicitly forces
regeneration. A request for a newer head is refused while an older head is running.
Code excerpts can receive keyboard focus; scroll horizontally to read long lines.
The Guide tab is read-only: return to **Review** to comment or approve.

A push makes the saved guide stale. On the next guide read, Station compares
its head SHA with the provider's current head and hides obsolete excerpts and
line notes. The guide's original SHA remains visible. Rewriting produces a guide
for the current revision; an old guide never counts as reviewing a new head.

Generation reads bounded Git blobs through an admitted repository snapshot,
without creating a checkout or running Git smudge filters. It gives the model
no tools and requests structured guide output. Station reads the merge-base-to-head change, so a
stacked pull request covers its own layer. Both exact commits must already be
available in the project's checkout; Station does not fetch missing commits.
Submodules follow
Station's repository-read policy and are not entered. Review conversations are
not supplied to the model, including resolved conversations.

Guides support up to 500 changed files, a bounded diff and context, eight model
stops, and an optional final stop naming files the model did not explain.
Invalid excerpt paths, ranges outside a diff hunk, or excerpts over 25 lines
fail generation. An excerpt longer than 25 inclusive lines fails the whole run
with a specific limit message; split long passages into shorter excerpts when
rewriting. Station runs at most two guides at once; additional requests
are refused so they can be retried later. Completed guides persist by forge,
repository, pull request, and head SHA across restarts. In-progress and failure
status is process-local; after a restart, choose **Rewrite guide** if needed.

Agents with bound operator authority can use `write_pull_request_guides` to
request a batch of 1–20 exact project/forge/repository/PR targets, and
`read_pull_request_guide` to inspect the result. An over-limit batch is rejected
before any request starts. Set `force: true` to rewrite an existing current-head
guide; otherwise it is reused. Capacity is checked before reading a forge
snapshot. Refused requests return an MCP error; a batch with any refusal is
marked as an error and retains every per-target result. Each admitted request
starts independently; a batch
can contain both starts and capacity refusals. These tools do not post reviews,
change source files, or approve a pull request.

Guides do not yet support project-specific instructions, generation by an
external coding engine, excerpt selection for comments, question-to-chat
actions, or a finish-review workflow. Questions are reading prompts only.

While a guide is running, the Guide tab polls process-local status every 15 seconds
without rereading the forge snapshot. It reads the full guide once the run settles.
Failures distinguish invalid model output, missing commits, oversized changes,
Git timeouts, storage limits, and changed access. Saved-guide read failures and
disabled-guide requests have separate messages from model failures. The preparation and model request
share a three-minute time budget. Guide generation disables VoltAgent's automatic model retries:
an excerpt-length failure is reported after the first attempt instead of being
replaced by a later generic error or timeout. Use **Rewrite guide** to try again,
or choose a model that follows the excerpt bounds.

documents.title: Work Board
documents.markdown:
# Work Board

Work Board is a personal Workspace Pane for arranging links to work you already
own in Station. It stores a reference and layout only. Titles, gate state,
receipts, and availability are always read from their owning feature.

## Pin and arrange work

Open a Project, choose **Add Pane**, then choose **Work Board**. Enter the
exact reference ID and any required owner scope. A Task's owner scope is the
exact Station Project **slug** (not its UUID); a Flow run's scope is the exact
Project ID. You can pin Projects, Tasks, Sessions, approval requests, gate or
Flow runs, scheduled outcomes, receipts, artifacts, and Agents. Station keeps
the typed identity you entered and never tries to repair a mismatched owner.

Each card keeps its linked title separate from its **Drag** handle, so opening
work never starts a move. Drag that handle to move a pin, and use the small
corner grip to resize it. Arrow keys move the focused handle; Shift+Arrow
resizes it. The ordered list is always available for keyboard use. In a narrow
Pane or on a touch device, it comes first and the canvas stays hidden until you
choose **Open canvas**; this avoids duplicate canvas controls in the compact
focus path.

Use the zoom controls to zoom in or out, or **Reset** to restore the default
camera. Drag an empty part of the canvas to pan. Motion is not animated when
your system requests reduced motion.

## Name, clean up, and restore

Edit the Board title and choose **Save title**. **Undo** restores the prior
Board snapshot. **Remove missing** appears for references reported missing by
the last loaded owner resolution. It removes pins, not the work they refer to.
Stale, ambiguous, unavailable, and unconfirmed results are not selected for
cleanup. Refresh before cleanup if the linked work may have changed: the
cleanup request checks the Board revision and pin identities, but does not
query each owner again.

The title, camera, pin geometry, and pin order are saved on the Station.
Returning to the Pane can reuse cached Board and resolution data; it does not
guarantee a new read. **Refresh Board** requests both again. A save uses the
Board revision shown on screen. If somebody else changes the Board first,
Station refuses the conflicting write and asks you to refresh. It does not
automatically show the other writer's changes. If a response is lost, the
result is unconfirmed until you inspect the Board again; Station does not guess
whether the mutation happened or retry it automatically.

## Linked work states

**Linked** means the owner could resolve the exact reference. **Not found**,
**Moved**, **Can’t load**, **Multiple matches**, and **Unconfirmed** describe
the last loaded owner resolution. **Unconfirmed** means an individual reference has not
yet produced a resolution; it is different from the visible resolver loading
or error notice. Use **Retry resolution** when that lookup fails. These states
are not copied status stored on the Board, and a linked item is not evidence
that a gate passed or work is complete.

For architecture and implementation evidence, follow the
[Work Board module](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/architecture/module-map.md#personal-work-board).
The refresh and cleanup recommendations are tracked in
[#2736](https://github.com/kontourai/station/issues/2736).

documents.title: Personal Boards
documents.markdown:
# Personal Boards

A Personal Board is your dashboard across Projects on one Station. It belongs to
your signed-in identity, so devices connected as that person see the same saved
Board. Its live sections read work you can access; saving a Board does not copy
Tasks, approvals or conversations into it.

## Create and edit

Choose **+** beside **Personal Boards**, name the Board, and open it. Start with
**Daily brief**, **Project watch**, **Review desk**, or **Start blank**. Project
watch asks you to choose an available Project first.

Use **Edit Board** to change its name and description, add or remove sections,
move sections up or down, and choose half or full width. Live sections can show
Tasks, items needing attention, recent Station work, or available Projects. Task,
attention and recent-work sections can filter by Project; list sections have an
item limit. Notes contain your own text. Links accept Station paths and HTTP or
HTTPS addresses.

**Preview** shows the draft with real live data. It does not save it. Choose
**Save Board** when ready, or **Cancel** to retain the existing Board. Leaving
with unsaved edits asks whether to discard them. Narrow panes and phone screens
stack the sections vertically.

Task and attention sections refresh about every ten seconds. Recent work
shares the session list: live stream updates invalidate it, with a 60-second
safety poll even while the stream is connected. Project sections refresh about
every fifteen seconds. Failed reads show Retry rather than an empty success. Attention can
report that an underlying source is unavailable. Links open the owning feature;
review and approve requests there. A Board never approves work on your behalf.

## Build through chat

Choose **Build with chat**. Station opens its new-chat picker without a Project
and offers the Board context as a removable draft. Choose an Agent allowed to
use Station Control, with `list_personal_boards`, `get_personal_board` and the
mutating `propose_personal_board` action enabled. In the Agent's **Tools**
section, choose **Add tools**, search for `propose_personal_board`, then open
the matching source to select its actions and review their approval choices.
Send your request after choosing the Agent.
If Station Control is unavailable to your Agent, use the visual editor.
The built-in Station assistant exposes these tools when ready and authorized.
For example:

> Make this my morning dashboard: pending decisions, active Tasks across my
> Projects, recent work, and a note reminding me to review the release.

The Agent can list and read Personal Boards, then propose a new dashboard or a
revision. It cannot apply that proposal through the authoring tools. An existing
saved Board stays visible until you choose **Review proposal**, inspect the
preview, and choose **Apply Board**. You can edit the proposal before applying
it, or dismiss it. A newly proposed Board is marked **(draft)** in the sidebar.
Proposals appear in an open Board within about five seconds; the sidebar list
refreshes within about ten seconds.

Follow-up requests such as “put recent work first” or “show only this Project’s
Tasks” use the same proposal and review path. If the Board changed since the
Agent read it, Station refuses the stale proposal. Ask the Agent to reread it.

Conversation and Task board faces use separate `board_pin` tools. Those tools
pin cards to that conversation or Task; they do not build the Personal Boards
listed in the sidebar.

## Recover and organize

If another device or chat changes a Board while you are editing, your draft
stays visible and Save is blocked. **Reload current Board** lets you inspect the
new version after confirming whether to discard your draft. A lost save response
may have committed: refresh and inspect the Board before trying again.

The Board’s sidebar menu offers **Rename**, **Open in** a region, **Move to
project…**, and **Delete**. Moving makes it a Project Layout and removes the
personal copy. If an interrupted move leaves two copies and either was edited,
Station retains both and asks you to inspect them; retrying cannot discard the
newer contents. Apply or dismiss a pending proposal before moving; unpublished
content cannot travel into a Project. Saved dashboard sections and existing
Layout tabs render in Main, a docked region, and the destination Project.

Existing Boards with configured Layout tabs keep those tabs when you add a
dashboard. Arbitrary plugin-pane composition still follows the existing Layout
and Workspace Pane contracts; the dashboard editor offers the bounded built-in
sections above. Instance-wide shared Boards are not part of this feature.

documents.title: Visual replies
documents.markdown:
# Visual replies

An Agent can publish a chart, table, diagram, collage or mockup as an HTML page
inside its chat. The built-in Station Agent already receives these tools. For
other Agents, configure the `station-control` attachment as described below. The shared registrations
are available through Claude Code, Codex and capable ACP connections. A
connection that cannot carry MCP servers reports that delivery limitation.

Ask the Agent to preview its page, inspect the screenshot, and publish the same
HTML. Preview returns a PNG, the content height at the requested width, and
console messages with stacks. It uses Station's existing Chromium acquisition
and a disposable profile. If Chromium is unavailable, install it through the
Browser workspace; publishing itself does not need Chromium. Preview checks the
browser's effective WebRTC policy before loading authored content. It refuses an
unsupported browser or enterprise override that prevents the restrictive policy,
even when the profile file requests it.

Local HTML and raster-image links in a Project conversation also open inline.
Station reads the file through that Project's workspace or a verified Git
worktree of the same repository. HTML uses the same isolated viewer; missing
or out-of-scope files show an unavailable message rather than navigating away
from the conversation. These file previews follow the current file bytes and
are not retained published pages.

Publishing writes to the conversation and may require engine tool approval.
For example, Codex configured with approval policy `never` can refuse the write;
select a session mode that permits approval. Station does not mislabel the
publishing tool as read-only to avoid that decision.

Pages appear at their tool result, remain outside collapsed tool batches, and
survive reload. They follow light/dark mode, support 50–200% zoom and an expanded
view. Expanding recreates the page and resets unsaved interaction state. Links
require recent interaction with that reply and confirmation before opening
outside Station. Browsers retain transient activation for roughly five seconds;
the request need not come from clicking the link itself.
The Open button waits 500 ms; Cancel mutes further link requests from that reply
until its viewer is remounted.

Scripts run in an opaque sandbox with no Station session or tool bridge.
CSP blocks ordinary network loads. Direct WebRTC constructors are disabled,
but a nested srcdoc frame can obtain a fresh constructor and send ICE UDP
packets in Chromium and WebKit. Published pages are **not network-isolated**:
they can disclose the viewer's IP or information entered into the page. Do not
enter secrets into a visual reply. Headless preview has separate profile-wide RTC routing restrictions and denied DNS/HTTP
egress; that protection does not extend to a viewer's browser. Preparation embeds quoted absolute PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP paths inside
the publishing session's workspace, including HTML `src`, CSS `url()` and JS
string literals. Captured bytes survive removal of the source image. SVG,
AVIF, unquoted paths and constructed JS paths are not embedded.

Use `--background`, `--foreground`, `--muted`, `--border`, `--accent`,
`--destructive`, `--success`, `--warning`, `--chart-1` through `--chart-6`,
`--radius`, `--font-sans`, and `--font-mono`. The viewer maps these to the current
Station theme; preview uses a fixed light or dark palette.

Source HTML is limited to 256 KiB, each image to 2 MiB, the expanded HTML to
8 MiB, and distinct images to 32. Height is 100–2000 pixels; preview width is
320–1920 pixels. Preview rejects content taller than 2000 pixels, screenshots
over 8 MiB, or console output over 128 entries or 64 KiB. At most two previews
run at once, with a 15-second render deadline and bounded process cleanup. V8's
heap is capped at 128 MiB; this is not a hard cap on the browser's total RSS.
Over-limit inputs and outputs are rejected rather than shortened.

A conversation can retain at most 32 pages and 32 MiB of serialized page data.
Pages belong to their publishing execution session. Closing or archiving work
retains them. Physical deletion of that session deletes its pages in the same
transaction; deleting every member of a conversation lineage deletes every
page in it. See the [security and deletion decision](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/decisions/html-replies.md).

## Which Agents receive the tools

The built-in **Station** Agent receives station-control's full catalog by
default, including visual replies, when its selected engine supports that MCP
passthrough. The runtime default Agent also receives the full catalog. Preview
and render are bounded writes on Station's auto-approved tool list; the engine
or session's approval mode can still refuse them. Preview runs in a disposable
browser with profile-wide RTC routing restrictions and denied DNS/HTTP egress. These controls
are separate from the accepted viewer-side WebRTC limitation above.

Other authored Agents, including direct Claude and Codex Agents, need the
built-in `station-control` MCP server attached. In the Agent's tool settings,
attach it and select `html_preview` and `html_render`. For Claude and Codex,
the equivalent configuration is:

```json
{
  "tools": {
    "mcpServers": ["station-control"],
    "available": ["station-control_html_preview", "station-control_html_render"]
  }
}
```

For an Agent using an **ACP engine**, attach the server without an `available` filter:

```json
{
  "tools": {
    "mcpServers": ["station-control"]
  }
}
```

ACP passthrough exposes the server's full tool catalog. Station refuses
per-tool `available` filters or disabled-tool selections on this path with
`engine-unsupported`; do not copy the Claude/Codex filter into an Agent using an ACP engine.
An ACP engine without MCP passthrough cannot use these tools. Merge server
entries into existing arrays rather than removing other tool servers. Start a
new conversation after saving tool settings. Authored Agents may optionally
configure auto-approval; otherwise approve the calls when the engine asks.
Codex policy `never`, for example, can refuse either call.

documents.title: Share an answer
documents.markdown:
# Share an answer

You can send someone a link to one answer from a chat. Anyone who has the link
can read that answer, without signing in, until it expires or you revoke it.

## Create a link

1. Under the answer, open **More answer actions** and choose
   **Answer details**.
2. In the **Provenance** dialog, choose **Share answer**.
3. Station copies the link and says it expires in 7 days. If the browser does
   not allow copying, the link stays on screen so you can copy it yourself.
   Station keeps no second copy of the link, so copy it before you close the
   dialog.

**Share answer** appears only for answers that carry provenance. You cannot
share from the desktop or phone app, or from an address that is not an
ordinary `http` or `https` address; open Station in a browser at a reachable
address first. A browser that is not paired yet is offered pairing first, and
pairing gives that browser full access to your Station.

## What the reader sees

The link opens a page that shows the answer's text as plain paragraphs and a
summary of how it was produced, such as which engine and tools were used.

- Only the answer's text is shared, up to 40 paragraphs of 20,000 characters
  each; the page says how many paragraphs were left out.
- Tool inputs and results, attachments and the rest of the conversation are
  not shared. Tools appear only by name.
- The page also shows the share's label and the conversation and turn
  identifiers.

The page reads the answer from your Station each time it is opened, so the
reader needs to reach the same address you used when you created the link. If
the answer has changed, the conversation is deleted, or you no longer have
access to it, the page says the answer is no longer available. A Station that
runs on your own computer is reachable only by people who can reach that
computer.

## Revoke a link

Open **Settings → Privacy & sharing → Shared answers**. Each link shows its
label (or "Answer from turn …"), whether it is live, revoked or expired, and
when it was created and expires. Choose **Revoke**, then **Confirm**. The link
stops working immediately and its page says it was revoked.

Revoked and expired links stay in the list. You cannot copy a link again,
rename it, or extend it from Settings.

## Limits

- A link lasts 7 days by default. Through the API you can set a label and a
  lifetime of up to 90 days.
- A Station keeps at most 500 links, including revoked and expired ones.
- A hosted Station does not offer answer sharing yet.
- Opening links is rate limited, so a page that is opened very often may ask
  the reader to try again later.

For the API and the security design, see
[answer share permalinks](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/design/answer-share-permalinks.md).

documents.title: Settings you may not have found
documents.markdown:
# Settings you may not have found

Most Settings rows explain themselves. This page covers four sections that
change what Station offers rather than how it looks. Open **Settings**, pick a
page in the left rail, or search for a setting by name. You can also find any
Settings row from the [command palette](../guides/keyboard-shortcuts.md#command-palette)
(⌘K or Ctrl+K).

| Section | Page | Saved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature previews | **Advanced** | On this Station |
| Developer tools | **Advanced** | To your account when you are signed in, otherwise on this device |
| Shared answers | **Privacy & sharing** | On this Station |
| Device hosts | **Devices** | On this Station |

## Feature previews

Feature previews are features that are still being evaluated. Each one has a
switch, a name and a description of what turning it on does. A preview is listed
only when this Station's build can run it; if none is, the section says
"No previews are currently offered". Previews start off.

The current preview is **Fleet consumer probes**: before routing work to a
model that another Station contributes, Station sends a test request to it.
That test can spend a completion on the other Station.

Turning a preview on affects everyone who uses this Station.

## Developer tools

**Enable developer tools** shows the **Developer** page in **Customize** and
the command palette, and its **Monitoring** page in the command palette. It is
off by default; a direct `/developer` link still opens when it is off.

Enabling it also reveals three independent previews: **Flow delivery preview**,
**Veritas readiness preview**, and **Trust preview**. Each starts off and is
saved on this device. The tools require both Developer tools and their own
preview switch to be on. Turning Developer tools off makes them unavailable
without clearing those saved choices. These device previews are separate from
the Station-wide Feature previews above.

## Shared answers

This section lists the answer links you have created, with their state and
expiry, and lets you revoke them. See [Share an answer](sharing-answers.md).

## Device hosts

A device host is another Mac or Linux computer that runs iOS simulators or
Android emulators for Station over SSH. Station uses your SSH agent and
configuration and never stores a key. Only the Station operator sees this
section, and only on a personal Station.

1. Confirm the host key once in a terminal: `ssh user@host`.
2. Choose **Add device host** and enter a **Name** and an **SSH target**, such
   as `me@build-host.example` or an alias from your SSH config.
3. Choose **Test connection**. Station checks that it can reach the host and
   that Node.js, Xcode simulators and the Android SDK are available.
4. Choose **Enable device hub** and confirm **Install and enable**. Station
   installs its device hub on the host under `~/.station-device-host`.

Each host's menu also offers **Share devices…**, **Disable hub**, **Edit** and
**Remove**. A Station can have up to 32 hosts. The
[mobile device workspace guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/guides/mobile-device-workspace.md)
explains what you can do with the devices once a host is ready.

## Nearby Stations

On the computer running Station, **Settings → Pairing → Discover this Station
nearby** makes its name and local address visible to nearby devices. It starts
off and only the computer's local operator can change it. The status below the
switch says whether publication succeeded; enabling it does not change your
network or firewall. Connecting still needs your approval. See
[Connect your phone](getting-started.md#connect-your-phone).

## Link to a setting

Every Settings row has a stable address of the form
`/settings?view=<section>&highlight=<row>`, for example
`/settings?view=feature-previews&highlight=feature-previews`. See
[Settings deep links](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/reference/settings-deep-links.md).

documents.title: Contributing to Station
documents.markdown:
# Contributing to Station

Use the route that best protects people and keeps a proposed change useful.
The [repository contribution guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
owns the current development and verification instructions.

## Choose the right route

| Need | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Report a defect or regression | Open a [bug report](https://github.com/kontourai/station/issues/new/choose) with the user impact, release/build identity, platform, frequency, recent change, redacted diagnostic, and nearest related issue. |
| Propose an improvement | Open a [feature request](https://github.com/kontourai/station/issues/new/choose) that explains the problem, workaround, core-versus-extension boundary, non-goals, and alternatives. |
| Discuss a broad or uncertain idea | Use the [issue chooser](https://github.com/kontourai/station/issues/new/choose). For a discussion/architecture proposal, use the feature form and state the decision needed before implementation. |
| Get help using Station | Use [Kontour support](https://kontourai.io/support/). |
| Report a suspected vulnerability | Use a private [Security Advisory](https://github.com/kontourai/station/security/advisories/new), never a public issue. |

## Keep reports safe and useful

Do not put secrets, access tokens, private URLs, customer data, or unredacted
logs in public reports. Use a redacted diagnostic ID or the smallest redacted
excerpt that explains the problem.

If you submit a pull request, explain the user outcome, the related issue and
closure condition, the evidence you obtained, anything `NOT_VERIFIED`, the
risk and rollback plan, and what you personally inspected. If AI tools helped,
identify the tools and material areas, then personally inspect the submitted
change; do not disclose prompts or private context.

## External forks

External-fork contribution execution is **NOT_VERIFIED**. This guide does not
claim that a fork check or hosted execution path is available or safe.

## Issue lifecycle handoff

Open an issue with the template that best matches the work. The reporter receives a clear handoff label: new and reopened issues begin at `needs:maintainer`; when a maintainer needs more information, they deliberately change that to `needs:reporter`.

Reply with the information that moves the issue forward—such as reproduction steps, environment details, or a decision. A substantive reply moves the handoff back to `needs:maintainer`. Reactions, acknowledgements, quoted text, and hidden comments intentionally do not change it.

Priority, delivery stage, assignment, claims, and closure are separate from this conversation handoff. See the repository [issue lifecycle reference](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/reference/issue-lifecycle.md) for the exact automation contract.

documents.title: Contribute to Station
documents.markdown:
# Contribute to Station

Use the [repository contribution guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
for the current contribution paths, review expectations, and verification
authority. This public guide is intentionally a short orientation, not a copy
of repository operations or delivery state.

## Contributor commands

The optional `just` interface is available on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
Install Just 1.44.0 or later with `brew install just` on macOS, `cargo install just --locked` on Linux when a package-manager install is unavailable, or `winget install --id Casey.Just --exact` in Windows Command Prompt. Confirm it with `just --version`.

Use Unix shell quotes for forwarded values, for example `just test 'name with spaces'`. In Windows Command Prompt use double quotes: `just test "name with spaces"`. The [generated contributor command reference](../reference/contributor-commands.md)
lists every supported recipe and its platform-specific command form.

The recipes are conveniences. The repository guide names the canonical command
and completion evidence for a contribution; a convenience command never creates
a second receipt protocol.

## Keep public contributions safe

Do not include secrets, access tokens, private URLs, customer data, or
unredacted diagnostics in public reports. Use the repository's security route
for suspected vulnerabilities. If AI tools assisted a change, disclose the
tools and affected areas in the contribution while personally inspecting the
submitted result.

documents.markdown:
# Keyboard shortcuts

Open **Settings → Keyboard shortcuts** to search Station commands by their
plain-language names.

- Select a shortcut, then press the new key combination.
- If the editor finds another registered command using it, Station explains the conflict before
  saving. Choose **Replace** to clear the old command and move the shortcut, or
  **Cancel** to leave both unchanged.
- **Clear** removes a shortcut. **Restore default** returns the command to its
  current registered default binding, which may come from a plugin or command skill.
- Each row has a context hint, with a technical hint under **Advanced**. These
  currently come from the command's ID, not its actual availability rule; they
  are not a live explanation of why a command can or cannot run.
  [#2767](https://github.com/kontourai/station/issues/2767) tracks that correction.
- Some known browser-reserved combinations carry a warning. They may work more reliably
  in the desktop app because a browser can intercept them first.

Shortcut changes are stored in this browser/app profile's versioned
`station-device-settings-v1` local-storage envelope. The older
`station.device-settings` record is a migration input. Overrides and command-skill
shortcuts are included in Settings export/import; they do not automatically
synchronize across Devices. The editor is read-only in the mobile layout,
including narrow desktop windows.

## Command palette

Press **⌘K** on macOS or **Ctrl+K** on Windows and Linux to open the command
palette from anywhere in Station, including while you are typing in a field. It
does not open while another dialog is open, and you can rebind it under
**Settings → Keyboard shortcuts**. There is no on-screen button for it, so a
phone or tablet without a keyboard cannot open it.

Type to search. Results are grouped into commands, actions (such as opening the
chat dock, a new Board, the tour or **Report a problem**), places to go,
plugins, Settings rows, open chats, Projects, workspace panes, Agents and
skills. After two characters it also searches indexed conversation messages.
Among close matches, items you use often rank higher; **Reset command history**
clears that. Choose
**Workspace search (this Station)** at the top to switch to workspace search.

Use the arrow keys to move, Return to run the highlighted item, and Escape or a
click outside to close. Running an item usually closes the palette and returns
focus to where you were. Some items keep it open, such as
**Reset command history**, which shows whether the reset worked, and a message
found on another Station, which explains that it cannot be opened here.

## Return in chat

Choose **Chat settings → Return in chat** on each device. Automatic uses Return
to send on desktop and to insert a new line on touch devices. You can explicitly
choose either behavior, including for an attached tablet keyboard. Shift+Return
always inserts a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Return sends. Return never submits during IME
composition. During a turn, the shortcut uses the composer's selected Queue or
Steer mode. This preference is included in device-settings export/import.

## Dispatch and limits

The registry orders matching shortcuts by priority, then registry order.
It checks the registered `when` expression and current input/modal state before
running a handler. An active modal suppresses global registry shortcuts;
Escape and chat shortcuts have additional input-ownership rules. A visible
row or saved binding does not bypass those conditions or a browser-reserved key.
A handler that returns `false` declines the key: it is not prevented, the next
matching shortcut is tried, and otherwise the browser keeps it. The Coding
stack's Back/Forward chords decline inside editors that own those keys
(CodeMirror, the terminal, a contenteditable editor) and when there is
nowhere to go; in plain text fields they are the stack's Back and Forward.

The editor's replacement dialog considers the first matching enabled command.
It does not analyze all conditional overlaps or guarantee that restoring a
default leaves every chord conflict-free. The catalog also depends on which
components have registered their commands in the current view.

Custom bindings containing Space currently store a key name that does not match
the standard keyboard event. [#2771](https://github.com/kontourai/station/issues/2771)
tracks the capture-to-dispatch correction; the defect was reproduced through
the mounted editor and registry with DOM events.

The [keyboard shortcut module](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/architecture/module-map.md#keyboard-shortcuts)
connects these rules to the editor, registry, device store, import/export owner
and tests. DOM/storage tests do not qualify every physical keyboard, OS shortcut,
or native shell.

## Plugin shortcuts

Plugins register shortcuts with the SDK's `useShortcut`. They join the same
registry under `plugin.<plugin>.<id>`, so they appear in the shortcut list
(under **Plugins**) and in Settings, and an active modal suppresses them like
any other. A plugin cannot replace a Station shortcut through the SDK,
because no Station id starts with `plugin.`. Plugin shortcuts rank below
Station's own, so a Station shortcut on the same chord wins whichever
registered first; only Station's "go up a level" Escape fallback yields to a
plugin. Only a verified plugin's pane can register shortcuts.

The command palette (⌘K), Settings (⌘,) and the shortcut list (⌘/) are
reserved, so a user can always get back in control of a misbehaving plugin.
So are the text-editing chords: ⌘C, ⌘V, ⌘X, ⌘Z, ⇧⌘Z and ⌘A, which are Ctrl
off a Mac, and Ctrl+Y.
Station refuses a plugin chord that equals one of their defaults or their
current bindings. If you later move a reserved shortcut onto a plugin's chord,
or move a plugin shortcut onto a reserved one, the plugin's shortcut stops
firing. Off a Mac, `cmd` and `ctrl` are the same chord for this check. A
plugin chord with no Cmd, Ctrl or Alt never fires while focus is in a text
field.

These rules apply to shortcuts registered through the SDK. A plugin that
runs inside Station's own page can still listen for keys directly, so they
are not a sandbox.

documents.markdown:
# Product-law authoring

Product laws are a small set of executable, user-observable invariants. Read
the [generated product-law reference](../reference/product-laws.md) for the
current public projection; do not copy its law table into explanatory guides.

## Choose a law deliberately

A law names a stable identity, an observable invariant, its owning module and
interface, and the owner responsible for remediation. It must have an exact
behavior observation and an exact fault observation. The contributor workflow
validates both observations from structured test output.

Affected-path disposition is explicit. A behavior change either matches a law
that owns the changed area or is recorded as deliberately outside the current
law set. Do not assign a nearby law by implication merely to make a review
look complete.

## Interpret the observation

- **PASS** means the exact behavior and fault observations both passed.
- **FAIL** means an exact observation failed and the owning behavior needs
  diagnosis.
- **NOT_VERIFIED** means a trustworthy exact observation was unavailable. It is
  not a pass and does not authorize completion.

**INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR** separately identifies a runner/deadline failure; it
is not a product assertion failure or a pass. The
[generated reference](../reference/product-laws.md) names the bounded law set;
the [testing guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/main/docs/guides/testing.md) explains evidence selection and execution.
The structured reporter must contain the exact selector once and passing; a
file-level exit, skipped test or nearby title is insufficient. These selected
laws do not prove every product invariant.

Product-law observations inform verification; they do not create a second
completion receipt. Follow the repository contribution guide for the current
authoring and verification workflow.

# Executable product laws

This file is generated from the product-law manifest. The manifest is the authority; this Markdown is a readable projection. Each law has exact behavior and fault observations evaluated through structured test results. A PASS means both named observations passed, a FAIL means either failed, and NOT_VERIFIED means the runner could not produce a trustworthy structured observation. The manifest is bounded to 6 laws, 6 test files, and 150s total runtime. None of these results create a second completion lane.

| Law ID | Observable invariant | Owning Module | Affected Interface | Behavior observation | Fault observation | Remediation owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `station.queue-dispatch.ordered-drain` | When a turn completes, Station removes exactly the queued head before canonical dispatch; a definitive 4xx rejection removes that head instead of requeueing it into a refusal loop. | `Chat queue drain` | `drainQueuedMessageOnTurnCompleted` | `pops the head synchronously, then dispatches the canonical Agent target after the settle delay` | `a definitive 4xx rejection drops the entry instead of requeueing and surfaces the failure` | station#613 |
| `station.lifecycle-completion.gate-derived` | A Flow run advances only when its gate evaluates matching evidence; completion is derived from that gate outcome rather than asserted by the caller. | `Flow run service` | `FlowRunService.evaluate` | `passes the gate and advances when claim evidence matches` | `routes back on failed evidence with attempt budget` | station#1555 |
| `station.approvals.actionable-resolution` | Only a known approval action can resolve actionable orchestration attention; an unknown action is rejected rather than failing open, and a real resolution marks the request actioned. | `Approval inbox` | `ApprovalInboxService` | `marks orchestration notifications actioned when the request resolves` | `rejects unknown approval actions instead of failing open` | station#1284 |
| `station.home-role.recovery-floor` | A granted Home renderer failure falls back to the built-in Home with the actual failure and a recovery action, never a blank root. | `Home role pane` | `HomeRolePane` | `a renderer that throws on mount lands on the built-in Home with the actual failure text` | `retry into a still-broken renderer lands back on the built-in, not a loop or a blank` | station#3122 |
| `station.release-stage.inventory-truth` | Release staging accepts only the complete required variant inventory, checksums, updater sidecars, and immutable container descriptor for one source identity. | `Release artifact inventory` | `validateReleaseInventory` | `assembles every required variant, sidecar, and immutable container` | `fails when uploaded bytes differ from the assembled checksum` | station#818 |
| `station.mobile-context.primary-actions` | Project and conversation switching remain directly reachable with readable context in the mobile dock header; opening a Project must not rebind the active conversation. | `Mobile chat dock header` | `ChatDockMobileHeader` | `keeps project and conversation switching directly reachable with readable context` | `opening a project preserves the active conversation binding` | station#1540 |

The contributor workflow regenerates this projection after intentional manifest changes. The gate rejects hand-edited projection drift, duplicate IDs, empty owners or selectors, nonexistent tests, a missing fault observation, and selectors absent from the exact structured test observation.

# Station shipped documentation

This is the canonical prose served by the credential-free Station Docs MCP.
The build compiles these topics and the architecture module sections into static
content. The interactive learning library reads the same Markdown. This manual
describes the product, not a particular Station's live state. Topic metadata and
stable IDs are maintained in [the topic catalog](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/learn/mcp-topics.json).

Update the owning implementation and tests when revising a claim. Run
`npm run docs:mcp:generate` after editing, then `npm run docs:mcp:check` to check
that the shipped content matches its sources. See [Learn Station](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/learn/README.md)
for navigation and [the audit ledger](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/plans/documentation-code-audit.md) for
remaining semantic review.

## What Station is

Station is an agent workspace for directing work, following execution, and
inspecting its results and available evidence.

An Agent's completion message is not proof that the requested outcome was
achieved. A Session or turn can complete without an evidence-gated workflow.
Flow gating is optional: the current start caller requires a Flow service, a
working directory, and an explicit non-retired `metadata.flowDefinition` before
attempting to attach a run. For attached work, inspect the actual gate verdicts,
evidence, exceptions, and unresolved checks. Report unverified claims plainly.

Station is local-first and does not require a cloud account for local operation. The Station-owned root defaults to `~/.station`; `STATION_HOME` selects one runtime home, such as `~/.station/instances/stable`. Persistence includes files and databases. Use the documented archive and recovery operations when moving a home; a directory copy is not automatically a consistent backup.

The core owns durable product responsibilities including Projects, Tasks, Sessions, authorization, execution, and evidence projection. Plugins extend the product through published contracts and admitted capabilities. The architecture learning tree explains these responsibilities and their interfaces; plugins do not acquire unrestricted access to core internals.

## These docs, and what they cannot do

`station-docs` serves this manual and the architecture topics as static content
compiled into Station. Its tools list topics, retrieve a topic, and search by
case-insensitive substring. They do not read user files, make network calls, or
require a credential at request time.

The returned version and documentation digest identify shipped content, not
live state. These tools cannot tell you which Agents exist, what is running,
what a job did, what a setting contains, or what is in a Project. Answer those
questions from an authorized live read, or state that only general
documentation is available.

`station-knowledge` is the separate data server for reading and capturing
Knowledge records. It requires caller authority; see [Knowledge agent tools](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/guides/knowledge.md#agent-tools).

`station-control` is the separate built-in server for Station operations, such
as creating Agents, running jobs, changing settings, and validating a local
plugin folder. Installing a plugin through Station's agent tools is refused: a person approves its preview on the Plugins page or with `station plugin install <source>` (see the `plugin-authoring` topic).
Control calls need an instance credential and remain subject to caller
identity, Session ownership, authorization, and approval policy. Delivering a
tool server does not grant full access or operator authority.

Station Docs needs no credential, but it still needs a supported tool-server
delivery path and the genuine shipped server. For example, the Muse adapter has
no MCP tool-server delivery channel. An engine with docs and no `station-control` can explain Station operations
but cannot perform them through the docs tools. The [connection guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/guides/connections.md) and
[Session API](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/reference/session-api.md) describe engine capabilities and delivery limits.
Say which capabilities are actually available; do not imply an operation ran
because its documentation was retrieved.

## Projects

A Project is Station's unit of working context and durable work identity. It can organize Tasks, layouts, Agents, knowledge, and settings, with explicit resources and machine-local workspace bindings where needed. An organizational Project need not have a checkout; a Task or Session that requires files must resolve an authorized available workspace instead of inferring one from a similar name.

Projects scope Agent selection. A Project can filter global Agents, and an
Agent may name an owning Project. Project-owned Agents are excluded from global
selection. A missing owner can be surfaced as an orphan finding instead of
deleting the Agent; if the Project inventory could not be read, the catalog
omits that finding rather than treating an unknown inventory as empty.

Projects present themselves as layouts — arrangements of panels for a particular way of working. Layouts can come from Station or from plugins, so a project page can be a chat surface, a review workbench, a readiness console, or a domain-specific vertical.

Open a Project's **Room** for shared discussion, notes, presence and explicit Agent requests. It is separate from a Task's Conversation and private Agent chats. Reading, discussion, note editing and execution require their respective current Project permissions and transport grants; Agent execution also needs host execution permission.

**Recap Project** prepares a prompt to review in the Room. Choose an Agent and
explicitly **Ask in room** to request a cited recap with freshness and coverage
limits. Preparing it does not execute work or replace an existing draft.

Use **Sources** to manage repository/folder bindings, Knowledge registrations, document imports and connections. Source registration does not grant execution or expose connector credentials. Project Knowledge registrations bind to the durable Project ID; an older unbound registration needs explicit operator attachment. Experimental S3 sources remain disabled by default pending AWS acceptance. See the [Knowledge guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/guides/knowledge.md) and [Project membership](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/design/project-membership.md).

Project resource resolution and a Task's captured workspace are different
records. The Task topic below describes the latter. See the
[system overview](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/architecture.md) and [work board](https://kontourai.github.io/station/docs/user/work-board.html)
for their ownership and navigation boundaries.

## Agents and engines

An Agent is the actor selected to do work. Its engine binding determines what
executes it and which authored capabilities Station can deliver.

Station's engine runs an Agent against a Model connection and supplies its
configured prompt, skills, tools, commands, and model within the runtime's
supported capabilities and policy.

An external engine — Claude Code, Codex, or a custom CLI engine such as OpenCode or Kiro — runs its own loop. There, the engine owns behavior and tools, and Station owns only the abstractions it can set for that engine (model, effort, thinking) plus whatever capabilities that engine has a channel to receive.

Engines use different transports, including native SDKs, headless processes,
and the Agent Client Protocol. The user-facing identity is the engine's name.
The runtime-owned Station Agent is a role, not a synonym for Station's engine;
its selected execution engine determines the available delivery mechanisms.

Each engine has a capability matrix for system prompts, tool servers, skills,
commands, and model selection. Requested authored content without a supported
delivery channel is reported as undelivered on the ordinary saved-binding path;
an absent request is not a failed delivery. Explicit `askBeforeUse` tool rules
are an exception: unsupported engines refuse the saved Agent as well. An explicit conversation engine
override must preserve required profile delivery and refuses unsupported or
undelivered content instead of starting a reduced profile. See
[execution overrides](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/reference/session-api.md#preserve-an-agent-profile-with-an-execution-override).

Use the [Agent guide](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/guides/agent-configuration.md) and [Session API](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/reference/session-api.md) for
current setup, capability, turn, idle, terminal, and recovery behavior. A matrix
entry describes a supported mechanism; it is not proof that a live engine
accepted a particular request.

## Connections

Connections separates Models and Engines. The Models tab contains Model connections; the Engines tab contains Engines. Choose the service or engine you recognize, then a model within it. Provider remains an implementation term, not the user-facing umbrella for both tabs.

A model connection is an LLM endpoint — a local Ollama, an OpenAI-compatible service, a gateway, or a cloud model service. It powers Station's own engine, which drives the inference loop itself.

An engine connection is how Station reaches an external engine that runs its
own loop. Station requests model and mode options supported by that engine and
projects its reported events; it must not promise that every engine accepts
the same model, effort, or thinking controls.

Station's engine drives a Model connection directly. External engines run
their own loops and may expose their own model catalogs. Their usable choices
come from the engine's capabilities and inventory, not the Model connection
list.

A configured, reachable local model is one credential-free option. Discovery, configuration, and readiness are different facts; inspect the Connections surface before assuming a detected service is ready for a conversation.

Startup can adopt detected Claude, Codex, and Muse engines with their default
Agents. An explicitly removed engine is not silently recreated. Adoption is
not credential or launch-readiness proof; use [Getting started](https://kontourai.github.io/station/docs/user/getting-started.html)
and [Connections](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/guides/connections.md) for that distinction.

## The built-in assistant, and what it needs

Station ships the reserved, non-deletable `station` Agent for operating the
workspace through Station Control. Its engine binding, model readiness, tool
delivery, and caller authority still determine which operations can proceed.

Its task guidance asks it to discover suitable installed skills and available
tools when useful, within the capabilities already supplied to it. Read-only
Station Control catalogs support that discovery where the engine can receive
them. This guidance installs nothing, enables nothing and grants no new access;
ordinary authored agents and direct CLI aliases retain their own configuration.


Its Station tools cannot install a plugin. An install is approved by a person who has read its preview — its permissions and the parts that run in Station’s own page — on the Plugins page or with `station plugin install <source>`. Asked to install one, the assistant points to that review. It proposes instead: `propose_plugin_install`, `update_plugin` and `remove_plugin` leave an ask that a person completes from Plugins.

That capability comes entirely from the `station-control` MCP tool server. `station-control` calls Station's own API, so it needs a credential for this running instance. A credential can only be handed to an engine over a channel that has been reviewed as not crossing the secret boundary.

Not every connected engine can deliver Station Control. Such an engine may
still chat, and may receive Station Docs if it has a supported tool-server
channel, but neither chat nor documentation access grants platform mutation
authority. These tool restrictions are not an operating-system sandbox; the
plugin-authoring topic retains that distinction for same-user shell access.

Inspect the engine picker's capability and readiness diagnostics before
starting the Station Agent. A connected engine can remain unable to deliver
its required control tools.

## Sessions, turns, and runs

A session is a bounded episode of agent work. It can be associated with a project, a layout, an agent, and an evidence-gated Flow run. Starting a direct chat creates a session; it does not silently create a durable Task.

A turn is one user-to-agent interaction inside a session. A turn may stream text, reasoning, tool calls, approval requests, and terminal or artifact events.

A run is the execution accounting: status, attempt count, retry eligibility, output references, and failure classification. An agent run is tied to an agent session; a scheduled run comes from a scheduled job instead of an interactive session.

Adapters project reported engine events into a shared canonical model.
Capabilities and available evidence still differ: an absent event, usage value,
or terminal result must not be invented to make engines look uniform. An idle
turn is not necessarily a terminal Session, and optional Flow gating must not
be inferred from ordinary execution completion.

## Tasks and the task workspace

A Task is a durable, user-addressable work identity belonging to a Project. It survives restarts and can span execution episodes. Sessions also retain persisted history; their purpose is to record an execution episode rather than own the durable work identity. A Task may correlate an exact Session, or none at all.

**New Task** on a Project, its Tasks layout, or Activity starts a shaping
chat in the normal composer, with a compact, removable **Shaping a Task** chip and the existing Project and Agent choices. Describe a rough idea or a clear one-liner. The
Agent can ask questions or return a proposal with a title, goal, **Done when**
checklist and suggested first step. Only **Create Task** on that card accepts
it: Station saves the Goal sentence as the description, seeds the complete brief into the shared Task document with the accepting person's document authority, and links the shaping Session without assigning an Agent or execution Session. After Start, the conversation keeps the full chat height; **Stop shaping this Task** in More removes the mode. Shaping mode persists through clarifying questions until acceptance or mode removal. A reloaded accepted card offers **Open Task**. A failed seed shows a recovery error; retrying acceptance reuses the same Task and preserves subsequent document edits. Ordinary direct chat creates no Task.

Choose **New Task from this** in a chat's More menu to shape that conversation immediately. Add any focus as your next chat message.
**Add to Task** offers **New Task from this** even when no Tasks exist;
it shapes the selected answer or input in the same conversation. The chat and
its existing answers remain available. An unavailable engine or malformed
proposal remains a chat, without an accepted Task.

This path currently uses Station's prompt/proposal format. It does not claim
to invoke Builder Kit, pass its breakdown gate, or file a provider work item.
Builder skills are discoverable from the installed Flow Agents package;
selected-agent delivery and a published structured shaping-result contract
are separate integration requirements.

A task carries typed references — to files, artifacts, receipts, sessions, runs, or external work items — and those references preserve exact identity. Similar titles or paths are not treated as correlation.

The Task workspace opens on **Overview**, with status, completion criteria, subtasks and kept deliverables. **Conversation** is the shared Task discussion, **Plan** holds the autosaved document, and **Work chats** opens separately authorized Agent conversations. **Details** retains workspace bindings, changed files, on-demand Basis, receipts and exact Session correlation. Opening the Task makes the viewer present. Explicit Agent requests can publish answers into the personal Task conversation; shared-member Task projection includes human messages and the document, not private Agent execution or answers. Linking a child Task or work chat does not publish it, grant access or complete its parent.

A Task's captured workspace is re-evaluated as `available`, `ambiguous`, or
`unavailable` when reopened. Available bindings permit the relevant local
inspection paths; changed or missing bindings preserve the recorded identity
without treating an old path as current authority. Dispatch has its own
readiness, ownership, admission, and durable reservation checks; an uncertain
remote start is not automatically safe to retry. See the
[work board](https://kontourai.github.io/station/docs/user/work-board.html) and [Session API](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/reference/session-api.md).

A task can also be dispatched: assign an agent or a skill to it and send it into a session. A Session dispatched for a Task receives a Task brief with its first turn: the Task, its linked tracker item, the Task summary, standing decisions, open questions, recent dead ends and a line per Session of the Task that its owner may read, with what it has claimed, pinned by a digest. What agents, people or the tracker wrote is quoted, as data rather than instructions. It re-reads the brief with the Station Control `get_task_brief` tool. While it leads the Task, or was requested from the Task room, it rewrites the Task summary with `task_summary_update` and records a keyed decision, question or dead end with `task_record`. Every earlier revision is kept, and neither tool changes Task status or the Task document. An open question puts the Task in Needs you until a person answers it. Opening a question as a non-lead Session, or answering one, also sends one message to the Task's lead Session through its conversation inbox: a new turn when it is idle, after its turn when it is busy, and nothing when the lead asked or answered it itself or has stopped. A person can also start a Task from a GitHub issue on the Project's board; Station copies the issue's description and latest comments into the Task document. Task statuses follow a neutral work-item vocabulary (todo, ready, triage, in progress, blocked, review, verification, done), plus a canceled state for work abandoned before completion.

An agent on any engine can declare a pull request it opened with the Station Control `declare_pull_request` tool; a person keeps the declared pull request onto a Task. A person can also opt a Task in to closing when its pull requests merge: with that opt-in, the Task moves to done once every pull request kept on it is merged at its provider. A pull request closed without merging does not complete the Task, a Task in todo, ready, triage or blocked never closes by itself, and no agent tool sets the opt-in. Station checks when someone with permission to change Task status refreshes the conversation's pull request links; nothing polls. A declaration is recorded when the turn completes and is lost if Station restarts first.

## Scheduled jobs and notifications

A scheduled job can use a cron expression, a fixed interval (`every`), or a
one-time timestamp (`at`); manual runs are also supported. The built-in
scheduler invokes an Agent with unattended-deny approval policy and records
its scheduler outcome.
See the [scheduler API](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/docs/reference/api.md#scheduler) for exact inputs and outcomes.

Scheduler receipts describe the observed execution outcome. They do not attach
a Flow run or prove the requested business result by themselves. Inspect the
recorded output and any explicitly attached evidence workflow before claiming
unattended work achieved its goal.

Notifications are provider-based: subsystems and plugins contribute notifications that Station aggregates, persists, and delivers, so a long-running or scheduled piece of work can tell you it needs attention.

## Skills

A skill is a reusable bundle of instructions and behavior that an agent adopts — a way to give several agents the same competence without duplicating a prompt.

Skills are a capability Station owns for agents it runs. For an agent bound to an external engine, whether the skill reaches the engine depends on that engine having a delivery channel for skills. Some engines do; others do not.

When an engine has no channel for an authored skill, Station records that as undelivered rather than silently dropping it, and the agent editor shows the authored content read-only with a diagnostic naming the engine that cannot deliver it.

Explicit conversation engine overrides refuse undeliverable required skills
rather than starting without them. Saved Agent defaults remain unchanged.

Skills are installed and browsed from the registry, like agents and tool servers.

A skill can also declare itself runnable as a slash command, which is how a reusable instruction sequence is invoked directly in a chat or assigned to a task. There is one authored concept here, not two.

## MCP tool servers, integrations, and tools

Station speaks the Model Context Protocol for tools. An integration is an MCP server that exposes tools; a tool is one callable function from that server.

The built-in Station Agent receives visual replies through its default
station-control attachment. For an authored Claude/Codex Agent, attach
station-control and select `html_preview` and `html_render`; ACP must attach the
whole server without an `available` filter. Preview self-contained HTML, inspect the returned screenshot,
height and console output, then publish the same HTML. Pages appear at the tool
result and survive reload. Use the host theme CSS variables. App/session access
and ordinary network loads are blocked. In the published viewer, WebRTC isolation is incomplete: nested
srcdoc can send ICE UDP, exposing viewer IP or data entered into the page. Do not
ask viewers for secrets. Preview and publishing are bounded writes and respect
engine tool approval. Chromium is needed only for
preview. See the [visual replies guide](https://kontourai.github.io/station/docs/user/html-replies.html) for byte,
image, viewport, time and retention limits.

Two built-in servers serve different purposes here. `station-control` exposes
Station operations as tools; `station-docs` serves static shipped prose without
credentials or live state. This is not an exhaustive server inventory: the
[Station Browser MCP server](https://github.com/kontourai/station/blob/3381f97163822db1c8e0b8f81a126fd840491f6d/src-server/tools/station-browser-mcp-server.ts)
has its own delivery and authorization boundary.

Before starting work, use Station Control's `search_conversations` to find
